Briefing

Letter from the Case Supervisor

The Bible Investigation Bureau · Department of Unsolved Antiquities

Two women share a house. Each has a baby son, born three days apart. In the night, one of the babies dies. By morning, both women claim the living child, and each says the other swapped the boys while she slept.

They lived alone — no servants, no neighbours in the room, nobody who saw anything happen. There is no document, no mark, no third person to ask. Nothing to weigh one woman's word against the other's.

This is the hardest evidence problem in the archive. Two identical stories, and nothing at all to tell them apart. Walk the house yourself. Look closely at what could — and couldn't — have happened inside it.

One thing before you start. A child died in this case. The file says so plainly and goes no further, and neither should we.

Mordecai ben Jair
Case Supervisor
Case Closed

The House Gives No Verdict

1 Kings 3:16–18

You've examined every wall, mat, and jar this house has to offer — and confirmed exactly what the letter warned you of: the house is airtight. One door, no windows, no witnesses, two identical rooms. There is nothing left inside these walls to settle the case.

That's the point of the story. The evidence that finally separates the two women doesn't come from the room at all — it comes from what each woman is willing to do to the child once a king proposes cutting him in two. The house was never going to solve it. A test of character does.
